# Local patch: tauri-plugin-barcode-scanner (iOS lens selection and torch)

This directory holds a modified copy of `tauri-plugin-barcode-scanner` 2.5.3, the official Tauri 2 barcode plugin. The patch has two parts: close-range focus (lens selection) and a persistent flash (torch) during a scan. Both live in the iOS Swift code. Two small supporting files also differ: `build.rs` and one permission file (see "What the patch changes"). The upstream JS API, the Rust sources and the Android code are unchanged.

## Why this exists

The project is a prototype that tests how fast and how reliably a Tauri 2 app can scan QR codes and barcodes with the camera of a real iPhone. The result is compared with a native implementation. The prototype is not a product.

During manual testing on an iPhone 14 Pro (iOS 27.0.1) a barcode held close to the phone could not be scanned, because the camera image was blurry and never came into focus. The code had to be 15 to 20 cm away before it scanned.

A second need came later: the app should offer a Flash button during a scan, and the flash must stay on until the scan ends or is cancelled. The plugin has no torch API. See "Part 2: torch" below.

## Part 1: blur at close range

Every iPhone lens has a minimum focus distance. Below it, no autofocus setting can sharpen the image. The main wide-angle lens of the iPhone 14 Pro focuses from roughly 15 to 20 cm. The iPhone 14 Pro can focus much closer (macro, a few centimeters), but only through its ultra-wide lens.

The system Camera app handles this by using a virtual camera that combines all rear lenses (`builtInTripleCamera`) and lets iOS switch to the ultra-wide lens when the subject is close. The plugin does not use that device.

What the plugin does, in `ios/Sources/BarcodeScannerPlugin.swift` (`setupCamera`) and `ios/Sources/Utils.swift` (`discoverCaptureDevices`):

1. It lists all cameras, physical and virtual.
2. It loops over them and assigns every rear camera to `backCamera`, so the last rear camera in the list wins.
3. The list follows the order of the requested device types, which ends with `builtInWideAngleCamera`. The plugin therefore most likely opens the main wide-angle lens. We did not log the chosen device, so this is inferred from the code and from the blur we saw on the device.

The JavaScript API cannot change this. `scan()` accepts only `cameraDirection` (`back` or `front`), `formats` and `windowed`. There is no option for lens, zoom or focus.

## What the patch changes

All changes are marked with `LOCAL PATCH` in the sources.

### Part 1: lens selection

1. **Camera choice** (`BarcodeScannerPlugin.swift`, `setupCamera`, and a new `backCameraRank` function in `Utils.swift`). Instead of "last rear camera wins", the plugin picks the best-ranked rear camera: triple camera, then dual-wide, then dual, then wide-angle. On an iPhone 14 Pro this selects the virtual triple camera, which lets iOS use the ultra-wide lens for close focus.
2. **Starting zoom** (same function). A virtual camera starts at zoom factor 1.0, which is the ultra-wide field of view. The patch sets the zoom to the first switch-over factor (`virtualDeviceSwitchOverVideoZoomFactors.first`), which is the main lens. The image framing therefore stays close to what the unpatched plugin showed.
3. **Focus range** (same function). `autoFocusRangeRestriction` is set to `.near` where the device supports it. This tells autofocus to prefer close subjects, which suits barcodes.

### Part 2: torch

4. **New command `set_torch`** (`BarcodeScannerPlugin.swift`, functions `applyTorch` and `setTorch`). It takes `{ enabled: boolean }`, finds the camera that the running capture session uses (`captureSession.inputs.first`) and switches the torch of that device. It rejects the call when no scan is running or the camera has no torch. On success it returns `{ enabled: boolean }`. The torch stays on until `set_torch(false)` is called or the scan ends.
5. **Torch off on teardown** (`destroy()`). Every way a scan can end (result, cancel, error) calls `destroy()`, which now turns the torch off before it stops the session. The flash cannot stay on after a scan.
6. **Registration** (`build.rs` and `permissions/autogenerated/commands/set_torch.toml`). `set_torch` is added to the command list in `build.rs`. The permission file defines `allow-set-torch` and `deny-set-torch`. It was written by hand in the format of the generated files, so a future regeneration of `permissions/autogenerated` would remove it unless `build.rs` still lists the command.

Why the torch is inside the plugin and not a separate plugin: the first attempt used the crate `tauri-plugin-torch` 0.1.0. It looks up its own camera with `AVCaptureDevice.default(for: .video)`. With our scan session running, switching the torch on froze the camera image and stopped scanning until the torch was switched off again. We think the torch plugin and the scan session held different device objects for the same camera, but we did not verify this with logs. Driving the torch from the device that the session already uses fixed it.

## How it is wired in

`src-tauri/Cargo.toml` contains a `[patch.crates-io]` entry that points `tauri-plugin-barcode-scanner` to `vendor/tauri-plugin-barcode-scanner`. The crate version (2.5.3) and the npm package `@tauri-apps/plugin-barcode-scanner` (2.5.3) are unchanged.

The app must grant the new permission in its capability file (`src-tauri/capabilities/mobile.json`): `barcode-scanner:allow-set-torch`. The app calls the command from JavaScript with `invoke("plugin:barcode-scanner|set_torch", { enabled: true })`, because the official JS package does not know this command. The call is only valid while a scan is running.

To go back to the official plugin, remove the `[patch.crates-io]` block from `src-tauri/Cargo.toml` and delete this `vendor/` directory.

## Status

Both parts are confirmed on the device. On an iPhone 14 Pro (iOS 27.0.1):

- The camera switches to the ultra-wide lens automatically when a barcode is held close, and the barcode scans.
- The Flash button turns the torch on during a scan. The camera image keeps running, scanning continues, and the torch stays on until the scan ends or is cancelled.

Both were checked by hand. Nothing was measured, and no other device model was tried.

To repeat the lens check: run `npm run tauri ios dev -- "<device name>"`, tap Scan, and move a barcode from 20 cm to about 5 cm over a few seconds. The image should jump to a wider view and stay sharp. Phones without an ultra-wide lens (for example the iPhone SE) have no macro option, and Part 1 changes nothing for them.

To repeat the torch check: tap Scan, tap Flash, and confirm that the light stays on and the image keeps updating. Then scan a code, or tap Cancel, and confirm that the light goes off.

## Android: a likely similar problem

This section comes from reading the plugin source. Nothing was built or tested on Android.

The Android half of the plugin uses CameraX 1.5.1 and ML Kit (`android/build.gradle.kts`). It selects the camera only with `CameraSelector.requireLensFacing(LENS_FACING_BACK)` (`android/src/main/java/BarcodeScannerPlugin.kt`, lines 159 and 179). It sets no zoom or focus mode, and it has no lens option either.

What follows from that:

- On phones where the system exposes one logical rear camera that spans all lenses (many Pixel, Samsung and Xiaomi models), the system may switch to the macro or ultra-wide lens by itself. This depends on the manufacturer and the model.
- On phones where the lenses are separate physical cameras, CameraX uses the main one, and a close barcode will be blurry just as on iOS.

Results from one Android device therefore say little about others, and the plugin gives the app no way to fix the problem. This patch does not touch Android.

The same limit applies to the torch. The published `tauri-plugin-torch` 0.1.0 calls `CameraManager.setTorchMode` on its own. A comment in the scan plugin (`BarcodeScannerPlugin.kt`, near `getActiveCamera()`) says Android rejects that call while a scan holds the camera. The torch has to go through the active CameraX camera instead, with `camera.cameraControl.enableTorch(true)`. The scan plugin already exposes that camera through `getActiveCamera()`, but the torch plugin does not use it. An Android `set_torch` would need to be written separately. It was not written or tested.

## Consequence for the native comparison

With a native implementation (AVFoundation on iOS, CameraX or Camera2 on Android) the app can choose the lens, the zoom, the focus mode and the torch. With the plugin it cannot, unless the plugin is patched or replaced. This gap belongs in any comparison between the two approaches. Each of these features cost a local patch to the plugin here, and someone has to keep that patch working when the plugin updates.

I searched crates.io and npm for alternatives. No Tauri plugin offers lens selection for scanning. `tauri-plugin-barcode-scanner-continuous` is a fork of the same plugin and uses the same camera selection.

## Other plugin behavior found while building the prototype

- On iOS, `scan()` does not ask for camera permission. It fails with "Camera permission denied or not yet requested". The app must call `requestPermissions()` first, and the capability `barcode-scanner:allow-request-permissions` must be granted.
- The `windowed` option behaves the opposite of what its name says. With `windowed: false` (the default) the camera view is placed above the web view and hides the whole web UI. With `windowed: true` the camera is placed below a transparent web view, so your own HTML, for example a Cancel button, stays visible. The prototype uses `windowed: true`.
